'''Sauerbrey:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = Governor | before_election = [[William Donald Schaefer]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Parris Glendening]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsMD}} The '''1994 Maryland gubernatorial election''' was held on November 8, 1994. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[William Donald Schaefer]] was ineligible for re-election. Prince George's County Executive [[Parris Glendening]] emerged victorious from the Democratic primary after defeating several candidates. Maryland House minority leader [[Ellen Sauerbrey]], who would also be the 1998 [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] nominee for governor, won her party's nomination. In the general election, Glendening narrowly defeated Sauerbrey by a margin of 50.21 percent to 49.78 percent, or by 5,993 votes, the closest gubernatorial election in Maryland since [[1919 Maryland gubernatorial election|1919]]{{cite news|last1=Rasmussen|first1=Frederick N.|title=Maryland's last cliffhanger was 1919 governor's race|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/11/10/marylands-last-cliffhanger-was-1919-governors-race-election-1994-2/|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=November 10, 1994}} and the first gubernatorial election in Maryland history to be decided by an absentee runoff.{{cite news|last1=Frece|first1=John W.|title=Republicans anticipated absentee role|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/11/09/republicans-anticipated-absentee-role-election-1994/|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=November 9, 1994}} Sauerbrey's campaign challenged the results of the election, filing a lawsuit alleging voter fraud and election irregularities; her claims were rejected by Anne Arundel Circuit Court Judge Raymond G. Thieme Jr. in January 1995.{{cite news|last1=Montgomery|first1=David|title=Judge rejects Sauerbrey's bid to overturn vote in Maryland|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1995/01/14/judge-rejects-sauerbreys-bid-to-overturn-vote-in-maryland/665e2a3e-21bc-43c5-a47e-9c007781faac/|access-date=March 10, 2024|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=January 14, 1995}} This election marked the first time since [[1915 Maryland gubernatorial election|1915]] that a Democrat won Maryland without [[Baltimore County, Maryland|Baltimore County]], the first time since [[1930 Maryland gubernatorial election|1930]] that a Democrat won Maryland without [[Cecil County, Maryland|Cecil County]], and the first time since [[1919 Maryland gubernatorial election|1919]] that a Democrat won without [[St. Mary's County, Maryland|St. Mary's County]].{{Cite web|title=Archives of Maryland, Volume 0126, Page 0249 - Maryland Manual, 1915-16|url=https://msa.maryland.gov/megafile/msa/speccol/sc2900/sc2908/000001/000126/html/am126--249.html|access-date=January 17, 2022|website=msa.maryland.gov}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x4tKAQAAMAAJ|title=Maryland Manual|date=1987|publisher=Hall of Records Commission|language=en}} This is the last time Howard County voted for the statewide loser. ==Democratic primary== ===Campaign=== Baltimore mayor [[Kurt Schmoke]], who was seen as the likely Democratic frontrunner in the race,{{cite news|last1=Banisky|first1=Sandy|last2=Bowman|first2=Tom|title=1994 governor's race heats up: Schmoke says he may enter|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/170654708/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=February 26, 1993|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}{{cite news|last1=Fletcher|first1=Michael A.|title=Schmoke moving fast, if not running|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/170654708/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=August 15, 1993|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} announced in September 1993 that he would not run for governor, instead opting for a third term as mayor in [[1995 Baltimore mayoral election|1995]]. Prince George's County Executive [[Parris Glendening]], Lieutenant Governor [[Melvin Steinberg]], and state senator [[Mary Boergers]] were among the first candidates to enter the race for governor. Governor [[William Donald Schaefer]], unimpressed with the early candidates, who were distancing themselves from Schaefer, encouraged state senator [[American Joe Miedusiewski]] and U.S. representatives [[Steny Hoyer]] and [[Ben Cardin]] to enter the race.{{cite news|last1=Tapscott|first1=Richard|title=Gov. Schaefer goes a-courting|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1993/10/20/gov-schaefer-goes-a-courting/bbd62d39-4533-4491-baea-7a2e12fff0e6/|access-date=March 8, 2024|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=October 20, 1993}}{{cite news|last1=Timberg|first1=Robert|title=Schaefer encourages 4 to enter governor's race In slap at current candidates, governor turns to 3 Democrats, GOP's Bentley|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1993/10/20/schaefer-encourages-4-to-enter-governors-race-in-slap-at-current-candidates-governor-turns-to-3-democrats-gops-bentley/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=October 20, 1993}} Although Miedusiewski entered the race a few weeks later,{{cite news|last1=Tapscott|first1=Richard|title=An unforgettable name goes on Md. ballot|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1993/11/17/an-unforgettable-name-goes-on-md-ballot/528ba32f-8460-4fdf-8210-2d1c89c50862/|access-date=December 13, 2023|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=November 17, 1993}} Schaefer declined to endorse him, saying that he didn't do endorsements, but urged voters to support him. Steinberg was initially viewed as the frontrunner of the Democratic primary, but his campaign suffered from poor fundraising and gaffes that contributed to his dwindling lead in polling. Glendening receiving the endorsements of both Schmoke and Montgomery County Executive Neal Potter established him as the new frontrunner in the race{{cite news|last1=Frece|first1=John W.|title=Glendening emerging as front-runner|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/05/29/glendening-emerging-as-front-runner-campaign-1994-the-race-for-governor/|access-date=March 9, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=May 29, 1994}} and gave him an overwhelming lead in the [[Washington, D.C.]] suburbs and Baltimore City, which led to his resounding victory in the Democratic primary in September 1994.{{cite news|title=Ideological opposites to vie in Nov. race for governor|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/09/14/ideological-opposites-to-vie-in-nov-race-for-governor-primary-1994-2/|access-date=March 9, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=September 14, 1994}} ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== * [[Parris Glendening]], [[Prince George's County, Maryland#County executive and council|Prince George's County Executive]]{{cite news|last1=Fletcher|first1=Michael A.|title=Glendening makes it official: He's in the race for governor|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/04/26/glendening-makes-it-official-hes-in-the-race-for-governor-campaign-1994/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=April 26, 1994}} ** Running mate: [[Kathleen Kennedy Townsend]], assistant attorney general for the [[U.S. Department of Justice]] and daughter of [[Robert F. ==Republican primary== ===Campaign=== Ahead of the election, Republicans expressed optimism in their ability to retake the governor's office,{{cite news|last1=Stuckey|first1=Tom|title=Md. has bumper corp of gubernatorial hopefuls|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/281279075/|access-date=March 6, 2024|agency=[[Associated Press]]|publisher=[[The Daily Times (Salisbury, Maryland)|The Daily Times]]|date=August 1, 1993|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} with party nominees receiving about 40 percent of the vote in recent elections{{cite news|last1=Smith|first1=Herbert C.|title=Potential Candidates for Governor, Their Strategies and Liabilities|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/170660003/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=August 15, 1993|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} and polls showing voters strongly disapproving of Governor [[William Donald Schaefer]] as a result of his support for an $800 million tax restructuring package and media coverage of his "style" problems, including his [[William Donald Schaefer#Governor of Maryland (1987–1995)|"shithouse" gaffe]].{{cite news|last1=Jensen|first1=Peter|title=Poll puts Schaefer's popularity at an all-time low|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1991/03/14/poll-puts-schaefers-popularity-at-an-all-time-low/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=March 14, 1991}}{{cite news|last=Rascovar|first=Barry|title=Maryland GOP Has a Chance for a 'Dream Team'|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1992/08/02/maryland-gop-has-a-chance-for-a-dream-team-2/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=August 2, 1992}} Potential Republican candidates predicted a crowded Democratic field to succeed Schaefer in 1994 and a resulting fratricide that would make coalescing around a single candidate following the primary elections challenging for the Democratic Party. Republicans also believed that the party was likely to nominate an urban-oriented nominee, which they saw as an ideal general election opponent. 1990 gubernatorial nominee William Shepard became the first candidate to enter the race, followed shortly afterwards by House of Delegates minority leader [[Ellen Sauerbrey]] in April 1993. Anne Arundel County Executive [[Robert R. Neall]], who was viewed as the early Republican frontrunner,{{cite news|last1=Jensen|first1=Peter|title=Neall names 26-member panel to gauge his election chances|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/373308908/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=September 19, 1993|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} announced in October 1993 that he would not run for governor, clearing a path for U.S. representative [[Helen Delich Bentley]],{{cite news|title=Bentley to decide on governor's race by Nov. 8|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/91902988/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Star Democrat]]|date=October 18, 1993|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} who announced her candidacy for governor a month later.{{cite news|last1=Timberg|first1=Robert|last2=Zorzi Jr.|first2=William F.|title=Bentley decides: She will run for governor GOP contender is a Schaefer favorite|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1993/11/10/bentley-decides-she-will-run-for-governor-gop-contender-is-a-schaefer-favorite/|access-date=September 20, 2023|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=November 10, 1993}} Sauerbrey steadily rose in polling during the Republican primary election, bringing the gap between her and Bentley within 13 points five days before the primary.{{cite news|last1=Frece|first1=John W.|last2=Timberg|first2=Robert|title=Tight race for governor seen in Nov.|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/09/14/tight-race-for-governor-seen-in-nov-primary-election-results-1994/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=September 14, 1994}} She also criticized Bentley as a "big-spending liberal", citing her voting record in Congress; Bentley did not respond to Sauerbrey's attacks and chose to keep a low profile at debates, instead focusing on the general election. Sauerbrey won the Republican nomination in an upset in September 1994, defeating Bentley by a margin of 52 percent to 38 percent. Sauerbrey's surprise win marked a rightward shift in the [[Maryland Republican Party]]'s politics and was one of many defeats for the Republican establishment, as voters rejected two of the state's three members on the [[Republican National Committee]] and defeated establishment candidate Richard Taylor in the comptroller primary election.{{cite news|last1=Goldstein|first1=Amy|last2=Tapscott|first2=Richard|title=A long shot, Sauerbrey hit mark in Md.|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1994/09/15/a-long-shot-sauerbrey-hit-mark-in-md/b6ecb019-2f6a-44e1-b604-e22beef3b706/|access-date=March 8, 2024|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=September 15, 1994}} ===Candidates=== ====Nominee==== *[[Ellen Sauerbrey]], minority leader of the [[Maryland House of Delegates]] from the [[Maryland Legislative District 10|10th district]]{{cite news|last1=Smith|first1=C. Sauerbrey continued to campaign on lowering taxes and deregulation.{{cite news|last1=Frece|first1=John W.|last2=Timberg|first2=Robert|title=Slim win may hamper Glendening administration|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/11/15/slim-win-may-hamper-glendening-administration-glendening-claims-victory-election-1994/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=November 15, 1994}}{{cite news|last1=Abramowitz|first1=Michael|title=Sauerbrey brings tax attack to Glendening's turf|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1994/10/06/sauerbrey-brings-tax-attack-to-glendenings-turf/f83ec328-66e9-4dc5-b3a9-40841ba9c456/|access-date=March 8, 2024|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=October 6, 1994}} In the final eight weeks of the election, Glendening spent $2.5 million on campaign ads portraying Sauerbrey as a [[right-wing extremist]] who would roll back protections on gun control and abortion rights, and associating her with televangelist [[Pat Robertson]] and his [[Christian Coalition of America|Christian Coalition]], who distributed campaign literature in churches spotlighting certain political positions of Glendening and Sauerbrey.{{cite news|last1=Babington|first1=Charles|last2=Shen|first2=Fern|title=Religious right's activism roils Md. governor's race|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1994/11/05/religious-rights-activism-roils-md-governors-race/5ab33a68-7e40-46c0-a918-0623554373dd/|access-date=March 8, 2024|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=November 4, 1994}}{{cite news|last1=Waldron|first1=Thomas W.|title=A Glendening ad stirs Sauerbrey's fury|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/11/05/a-glendening-ad-stirs-sauerbreys-fury-campaign-1994-the-race-for-governor/|access-date=March 8, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=November 5, 1994}} He also criticized her pledge to cut taxes, calling her a "millionairess" and arguing that it would curtail essential state services and force local jurisdictions to compensate by raising property taxes. As a result of the ad blitz, Sauerbrey's approval ratings fell into the 30 percent range within the final days of the election. (United States) |swing = }} {{Election box end}} ===Dispute over results=== On November 12, 1994, Sauerbrey's campaign said that it had hired sixteen professional investigators, led by attorney [[George Beall (attorney)|George Beall]] and party counsel [[Chris West (politician)|Chris West]], to probe complaints of voter fraud and irregularities in the gubernatorial general election.{{cite news|last1=Timberg|first1=Robert|last2=Waldron|first2=Thomas W.|title=Glendening on brink of win Sauerbrey says she may not close gap of 2,543 votes|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/11/12/glendening-on-brink-of-win-sauerbrey-says-she-may-not-close-gap-of-2543-votes-election-1994/|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=November 12, 1994}}{{cite news|title=Challenge in governor's race uncharted territory Lawyers research candidate options|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/11/12/challenge-in-governors-race-uncharted-territory-lawyers-research-candidate-options-election-1994-2/|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=November 12, 1994}} The investigation claimed that voting machines in Prince George's and Montgomery counties and the city of Baltimore had been tampered with to record votes from 4,774 incarcerated individuals, 37 dead voters, 71 individuals who provided elections officials with addresses of vacant buildings, 20 unregistered voters, and 84 voters who had voted twice. Sauerbrey filed an unprecedented{{cite news|last1=Frece|first1=John W.|title=Sauerbrey suit over election is put on fast track|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/12/29/sauerbrey-suit-over-election-is-put-on-fast-track/|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=December 29, 1994}} lawsuit seeking to overturn the general election results, citing the findings of her investigation and earlier claims that about 2,000 absentee ballots were cast without a required affidavit or processed early by election officials.{{cite news|last1=Frece|first1=John W.|last2=Zorzi|first2=William F. Jr.|title=11,000 votes challenged Republican Ellen Sauerbrey officially files suit contesting November election|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/12/28/11000-votes-challenged-republican-ellen-sauerbrey-officially-files-suit-contesting-november-election/|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=December 28, 1994}}{{cite news|last1=Janofsky|first1=Michael|title=Loser for Maryland Governor Files Suit to Overturn Election|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/12/29/us/loser-for-maryland-governor-files-suit-to-overturn-election.html|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=December 29, 1994}} Lawyers for the Glendening campaign sought to dismiss Sauerbrey's lawsuit, saying that the alleged voting irregularities were "the result of [at worst] excusable neglect, or do not involve intentionally wrongful acts or acts of fraud by voters, election officials, or others" and that Sauerbrey could not prove that such voters cast ballots for Glendening or voted in the governor's race at all. Maryland attorney general [[J. Joseph Curran Jr.]] also sought the dismissal of the lawsuit, saying that the [[Constitution of Maryland]] gave the [[Maryland House of Delegates]] exclusive jurisdiction over deciding the outcome of a disputed gubernatorial election.{{cite news|last1=Frece|first1=John W.|title=Glendening seeks dismissal of Sauerbrey suit|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1994/12/31/glendening-seeks-dismissal-of-sauerbrey-suit/|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=December 31, 1994}} On January 14, 1995, Anne Arundel Circuit Court Judge Raymond G. Thieme Jr. rejected Sauerbrey's claims, saying that while the Maryland Republican Party's investigation of the election presented "serious problems in Baltimore City", Sauerbrey presented no "clear and convincing" proof of election fraud. Sauerbrey initially planned to appeal Judge Thieme's decision, but withdrew her appeal on January 16, 1995.{{cite news|last1=James|first1=Michael|title=Sauerbrey abandons election appeal|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/1995/01/16/sauerbrey-abandons-election-appeal/|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[The Baltimore Sun]]|date=January 16, 1995}} In November 2020, in an interview with ''[[Maryland Matters]]'' after President [[Donald Trump]] made [[Attempts to overturn the 2020 United States presidential election|false claims about voter fraud in the 2020 presidential election]], Sauerbrey expressed no regrets about challenging her 1994 election outcome.{{cite news|last1=Rydell|first1=John|title=Glendening, Sauerbrey Reflect on the Ballot Impasse - And Their Own|url=https://www.marylandmatters.org/2020/11/07/glendening-sauerbrey-reflect-on-the-ballot-impasse-and-their-own/|access-date=March 10, 2024|work=[[Maryland Matters]]|date=November 7, 2020}} == Notes == {{notelist}} '''Partisan clients'''
